content.overview: Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is the principal fault-based and status-based divorce provision. Either spouse may petition on grounds including adultery, cruelty, desertion for two years, conversion, incurable unsoundness of mind / mental disorder, venereal disease in a communicable form, renunciation of the world, and presumption of death (seven years). The wife has additional grounds under s. 13(2). Section 13A permits the Court to grant judicial separation instead of divorce. Mutual consent is a separate route under s. 13B.
content.glance: HMA s. 13 — fault/status divorce grounds for either spouse; s. 13(2) wife’s grounds; s. 13A judicial separation alternate; s. 13B mutual consent is separate.
content.study:
Section 13 is the core contested-divorce provision of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

Sub-section (1) grounds for either spouse: (i) adultery; (ia) cruelty; (ib) desertion for continuous two years; (ii) conversion; (iii) incurable unsoundness of mind / mental disorder; (v) venereal disease in communicable form; (vi) renunciation of the world; (vii) presumption of death (seven years).

Sub-section (2) — additional grounds for the wife only.
Section 13A — Court may grant judicial separation instead of divorce.
Section 13B — separate mutual-consent route.
Cruelty and desertion are the most examined grounds. Irretrievable breakdown is not an independent statutory ground under s. 13.

sections.heading: Provenance and scheme
sections.body: Section 13 was expanded by the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976 (cruelty and desertion as independent grounds). Divorce under s. 13 requires proof of a listed ground; it coexists with s. 13B mutual consent and ss. 9–10 restitution/judicial separation.

sections.heading: Textual anatomy of s. 13(1)
sections.body: (i) adultery; (ia) cruelty (physical or mental); (ib) desertion — two years continuous, factum and animus deserendi, without petitioner’s consent; (ii) conversion; (iii) mental disorder of such kind/extent that cohabitation cannot reasonably be expected; (v)–(vii) venereal disease, renunciation, presumption of death.

sections.heading: Proving ingredients
sections.body: Valid marriage; proof of chosen ground; for desertion full two-year period with animus; for cruelty conduct meeting the legal standard; petition by aggrieved spouse.

sections.heading: Evidence and forum
sections.body: Petitioner bears the burden on a preponderance of probabilities. Family Court / District Court under HMA and Family Courts Act. Bars include accessory, connivance, condonation, collusion subject to the statutory scheme.

sections.heading: s. 13A and contrast with s. 13B
sections.body: s. 13A allows judicial separation instead of divorce where just. s. 13B is joint mutual-consent divorce and must not be confused with fault-based s. 13.

examples.title: Mental cruelty
examples.body: Continuous false allegations, public humiliation, and denial of marital obligations causing reasonable apprehension of harm — s. 13(1)(ia) maintainable.

examples.title: Incomplete desertion period
examples.body: Separation of eighteen months — s. 13(1)(ib) petition premature.

hypotheticals.question: If cruelty is proved, what happens to a competing restitution petition under s. 9?
hypotheticals.analysis: Withdrawal is with reasonable excuse; restitution fails; same finding supports divorce under s. 13(1)(ia) or judicial separation under s. 13A.

distinctions.title: s. 13 vs s. 13B
distinctions.right: Mutual consent; joint petition; living separately one year or more.

misconceptions.trap: Irretrievable breakdown is an independent statutory ground under s. 13.
misconceptions.correction: It is not listed. Courts may consider prolonged hostility when assessing cruelty under s. 13(1)(ia).

misconceptions.trap: Citing ‘Section 13’ without the clause is enough.
misconceptions.correction: Always cite the precise clause and name the Act.

cases.name: Naveen Kohli v. Neelu Kohli
cases.facts: Prolonged mutual hostility and breakdown over many years.
cases.issue: Whether prolonged hostility justifies divorce on cruelty under s. 13(1)(ia).
cases.ratioDecidendi: Prolonged mutual hostility and separation can constitute mental cruelty; irretrievable breakdown is relevant to assessing cruelty though not an independent statutory ground.
cases.holding: Divorce on cruelty; legislative recognition of irretrievable breakdown recommended.
cases.relevance: Leading mental cruelty orientation; verification gate open.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Enumerate the principal grounds under HMA s. 13(1).
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Adultery; cruelty; desertion two years; conversion; mental disorder; venereal disease communicable; renunciation; presumption of death seven years. Note s. 13(2), s. 13A, contrast s. 13B.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Enumerate and briefly explain the principal grounds of divorce under Section 13(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: State each s. 13(1) ground with clause cite. Note s. 13(2) wife’s grounds; s. 13A; contrast s. 13B. State irretrievable breakdown is not an independent statutory ground.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Discuss divorce under Section 13 HMA 1955. Examine cruelty and desertion; distinguish s. 13B.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Scheme and 1976 expansion. II. Full s. 13(1) grounds. III. Cruelty deep-dive. IV. Desertion deep-dive. V. s. 13(2). VI. s. 13A. VII. vs s. 13B. VIII. Bars. IX. Conclusion.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Submissions on mental cruelty under s. 13(1)(ia) with competing s. 9 petition.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Plead cumulative conduct; show reasonable excuse defeating restitution; seek divorce or s. 13A; rely on mental cruelty orientation authorities only as verified.
